## Introduction & background

CMOS (Complementary Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor) logic is the foundation of modern digital ICs. A basic CMOS inverter is constructed by stacking a PMOS pull-up transistor on top of an NMOS pull-down transistor. Because they require opposite gate voltages to turn on, only one transistor conducts at a time when the input is held solidly high or solidly low. This ensures there is almost zero static DC power dissipation. However, during a state transition, both transistors briefly conduct, and the capacitive load of the output must be charged or discharged. This results in brief spikes of current, known as dynamic switching loss, which scales linearly with the switching frequency.

## Core equations

Dynamic Power Dissipation:
$$P_{dynamic} = C_{load} V_{DD}^2 f$$

## What you're building

1. A discrete CMOS inverter built from scratch using a BS250 PMOS and a 2N7000 NMOS.
2. A manual parameter-sweep setup to plot the inverter's Voltage Transfer Curve (VTC) by stepping the input from 0 to 5 V in 0.25 V increments.
3. A static power test using a multimeter to measure the supply current at stable states (0 V and 5 V) versus right at the switching threshold.
4. A high-speed ring oscillator built by daisy-chaining three CD40106 inverters to measure high-frequency oscillation and observe dynamic power loss.

## Activity

Build an inverter: BS250 on top, 2N7000 on the bottom, gates tied as input, drains tied as output, 5 V rail. Step Vin 0→5 V in 0.25 V steps, log Vout — plot the transfer curve. Measure supply current at Vin = 0 V, 5 V, and right at the switching threshold. Then wire 3 CD40106 inverters in a ring; measure the oscillation frequency.

## Question to answer

1. Why is the static current ~zero in both stable logic states (trace the nonexistent DC path)?
2. Where exactly does the power go when the circuit is rapidly switching (Estimate $P = C \cdot V^2 \cdot f$ for your ring oscillator)?
